title: Accessibility
description: Accessibility information for Shai Zaidenberg’s personal website.
keywords: ← Back Home / Accessibility ACCESSIBILITY Designed for more people. Updated 15 November 2026 Our approach The site is designed with WCAG 2.2 Level AA in mind. This statement describes the implementation and testing, not an independent certification or a claim that every legal requirement is satisfied. Display controls The accessibility icon on every page opens controls for text size, higher contrast, reduced motion, underlined links, and text spacing. A reset option restores the defaults. The header provides dark and light themes. These controls supplement the underlying accessible design; they do not replace it. Keyboard and screen readers The site uses semantic landmarks, heading hierarchies, labeled controls, visible focus, a skip link, and native dialogs. Escape closes the accessibility panel and focus returns to its opening control. Navigation, the Explore menu, news and glossary filters, pagination, playbook checklists, the Analyst Toolkit, diagram step controls, and fictional walkthroughs are keyboard operable. Every architecture diagram has a text description and its steps are listed as text beneath it. Dynamic results are announced as status updates. Motion and media System reduced-motion preferences take priority. The site avoids flashing content. Decorative motion, such as the slow ambient background, the orbit model, and the flowing lines in diagrams, can be paused at any time and is switched off when your system requests reduced motion. Videos never autoplay and use native playback controls. They are silent, and each has a written transcript that supplies its meaning without requiring playback. Imagery is illustrative, and meaningful images have alternatives. Known limits Checks cover responsive layouts, core contrast, links, and representative keyboard interactions. Comprehensive testing with assistive technology and people with disabilities has not been completed. The news search, the Analyst Toolkit, and diagram stepping require JavaScript; without it, diagram captions are listed in full and the catalog source link remains available. On small screens the diagrams scroll sideways. Translucent surfaces switch to solid ones in higher-contrast mode or when your system requests reduced transparency. External sites are outside this site’s control. Report an issue Email shaizaidenberg@gmail.com with the page, problem, and any browser or assistive technology details you are comfortable sharing. You can request the information in another format. Animation controls The header contains a Pause motion button. It controls the ambient background, decorative orbit animation, scrolling and page transitions, diagram walkthroughs, and other motion throughout the site. The homepage also offers a Pause animation control next to the investigation model. Both use the same saved preference as Reduce motion in the accessibility panel. Your system’s reduced-motion setting always takes priority.

title: Architecture Blueprints
description: Animated reference architectures for security operations: the detection pipeline, the incident response lifecycle, an AI agent with guardrails, and zero trust access.
keywords: ← Back Home / Blueprints ARCHITECTURE BLUEPRINTS See the system. Then defend it. Four reference architectures for security operations, drawn as animated diagrams you can step through. Generic patterns built on public standards, not a description of any real environment. 01 From telemetry to decision 02 The response lifecycle 03 An agent with boundaries 04 Access without implicit trust 05 Watch the films DETECTION & RESPONSE From telemetry to decision. A reference flow for a detection program. Each stage depends on the one before it, and the last stage feeds the first. 01 From telemetry to decision. Flow diagram: five telemetry sources feed collection and normalization, then detection, triage, response, and a learning loop that tunes detection. Endpoints Identity Cloud Network SaaS apps Collect & normalize Common schema, asset and identity context Searchable history Retention for hunting Detect Rules, correlation, anomalies Triage Analyst, with AI assistance Respond Approved, reversible actions Learn Tune rules, close gaps 01 Sources 02 Collect and normalize 03 Detect 04 Triage 05 Respond 06 Learn Play walkthrough Sources Telemetry from endpoints, identity, cloud, network, and SaaS. A coverage gap here is invisible to every later stage. Collect and normalize Events are parsed into a common schema, given asset and identity context, and kept as searchable history for hunting. Detect Rules, correlation, and anomaly logic turn events into alerts. Each rule needs an owner, a test, and a reason to exist. Triage An analyst, supported by automation and past context, separates evidence from assumption and decides what the alert means. Respond Containment uses approved, reversible actions. A person authorizes anything consequential. Learn Every case feeds back: tune noisy rules, add missing telemetry, and record what the next analyst will need. INCIDENT RESPONSE The response lifecycle. The working loop behind every playbook on this site, following NIST SP 800-61 and the CSF 2.0 functions. Governance sits at the center of all six phases. 02 The response lifecycle. Cycle diagram: prepare, detect and analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, and improve, arranged around a central governance function, with improvement feeding preparation. Prepare Roles, access, exercised playbooks Detect & analyze Confirm, scope, set severity Contain Limit damage, preserve evidence Eradicate Remove access and root cause Recover Restore, verify, monitor Improve Review, fix, update playbooks Govern Roles, policy, risk 01 Prepare 02 Detect and analyze 03 Contain 04 Eradicate 05 Recover 06 Improve Play walkthrough Prepare Roles, contacts, access, tooling, and exercised playbooks exist before the incident. Preparation decides how the first hour goes. Detect and analyze Confirm that it is an incident, set severity, scope the affected systems, and start a timeline. Contain Limit the damage while preserving evidence. Fast isolation first, durable containment next. Eradicate Remove the attacker’s access: persistence, accounts, tooling, and the weakness that let them in. Recover Restore from trusted sources in priority order, verify the result, and monitor for a return. Improve Review without blame. Turn findings into detections, fixes, and updated playbooks, which is where preparation begins again. AI FOR DEFENDERS An agent with boundaries. A pattern for giving an AI assistant a useful job in security operations without giving it the keys. The controls are enforced in code around the model, not inside its prompt. 03 An agent with boundaries. Architecture diagram: an alert goes to an AI agent that queries read-only tools, passes through a policy gate and human approval before any action, and produces an evidence report and an audit log. READ-ONLY TOOLS Alert One defined task AI agent Plans and reasons. No standing credentials. Log search Endpoint data Threat intelligence Policy gate Allows reads, holds writes Human approval Required for any change Action Reversible Evidence report Sources, confidence, open questions Audit log Every prompt, tool call, and decision 01 A defined task 02 The agent 03 Read-only tools 04 Policy gate 05 Human approval 06 The record Play walkthrough A defined task One alert, one job. The agent’s scope is that task and nothing broader. The agent The model plans and reasons. It holds no standing credentials of its own. Read-only tools Evidence is gathered through narrow, read-only queries. Tool output is treated as data, never as instruct

title: Cyber Glossary
description: Search 26 plain-language cybersecurity terms across identity, detection, operations, intelligence, AI, and vulnerabilities.
keywords: ← Back Home / Cyber Glossary THE CYBER GLOSSARY Shared language. Sharper conversations. Plain-language explanations of terms used across this site. A practical starting point, without the acronym overload. Find a term All terms AI security Detection Identity Intelligence Operations Risk Vulnerabilities 26 terms shown Operations Alert triage The first review of an alert to establish its meaning, priority, and next investigation step. In practice A starting assessment should identify supporting evidence and unresolved questions. Risk Asset inventory A record of the systems, software, identities, and services an organization operates. In practice An advisory becomes actionable when it can be connected to an actual asset and owner. Risk Attack surface The exposed paths through which someone could interact with or attempt to compromise a system. In practice Reachable services, identities, software interfaces, and trust relationships all matter. Identity Authentication The process of verifying a claimed identity. In practice Successful authentication does not automatically establish that the activity was legitimate. Identity Authorization The decision about what an authenticated identity is permitted to do. In practice Authentication and permission are separate questions. Detection Baseline A reference pattern used to compare current behavior with expected activity. In practice A changed pattern is a lead to investigate, not automatically a malicious event. Operations Containment Response measures intended to limit further harm or spread during an incident. In practice Choose and verify measures through the authorized response process. Vulnerabilities CVE A Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures identifier for a publicly disclosed vulnerability. In practice An identifier helps connect advisories and references; it does not determine your organization’s risk by itself. Vulnerabilities CVSS The Common Vulnerability Scoring System describes technical characteristics and severity of vulnerabilities. In practice A score is one input to prioritization, alongside exposure, exploitation, and business context. Detection Detection engineering The practice of designing, testing, maintaining, and improving security detections. In practice Good detection logic depends on reliable source data and meaningful validation. Operations EDR Endpoint Detection and Response tools collect endpoint activity and support investigation and response. In practice Tool presence alone does not prove that a relevant event was observed or blocked. Detection False positive A result treated as a detection match even though the behavior of interest did not occur. In practice Document the reason for the classification before changing a rule. Intelligence Indicator of compromise An observable artifact, such as a domain or file hash, that may be associated with malicious activity. In practice Indicator reputation should be interpreted alongside telemetry and context. Vulnerabilities KEV CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog identifies vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation in the wild. In practice Catalog inclusion supports prioritization; absence from the catalog does not establish safety. Identity Least privilege Granting only the permissions needed for a particular responsibility. In practice Apply it to people, services, and AI tools, and review access as responsibilities change. Identity MFA Multi-factor authentication uses more than one type of authentication factor. In practice Its effectiveness depends on the method, configuration, enrollment, and recovery paths. Operations Observability The ability to understand system behavior through available outputs such as logs, metrics, and traces. In practice Missing or stale telemetry limits what an investigation can conclude. Operations Playbook A documented process for handling a particular operational or security scenario. In practice A playbook should identify decision points, responsibilities, and verification steps. AI security Prompt injection Untrusted content attempts to influence an AI system’s behavior or redirect its task. In practice Treat retrieved material as data, and keep tool permissions and sensitive actions under independent controls. Intelligence Provenance Information about where an artifact, claim, or piece of evidence came from. In practice Source and collection context help an analyst assess reliability. Risk Risk The potential for harm considered in the context of likeliho

title: Give agents a job. Give them a boundary.
description: An impressive answer is only part of an AI workflow. Permissions, evidence, and review paths determine whether the system is useful.
keywords: ← Back Home / Fieldnotes / Give agents a job. Give them a boundary. RESPONSIBLE AUTOMATION Give agents a job. Give them a boundary. An impressive answer is only part of an AI workflow. Permissions, evidence, and review paths determine whether the system is useful. By Shai Zaidenberg · Practical perspective · 5 November 2026 Define a narrow responsibility. A useful assistant has a specific input, a clear output, and a known set of tools. Triage, enrichment, and documentation are different jobs. Separating them makes it easier to evaluate results and understand where a mistake occurred. Keep untrusted material in its place. Logs, documents, and external reports are data, not authority to change the workflow. Tool access should match the task. Sensitive actions deserve explicit review, with enough evidence for a person to make an informed decision. Make uncertainty part of the output. State which sources were checked, which were unavailable, and which conclusions are inferred. An assistant that says “I could not verify this” is more useful than one that quietly turns an information gap into confidence. These are general engineering principles, not an assessment of a particular organization. Validate assumptions against your environment. Back to all insights

title: Turn “critical” into a decision.
description: A published severity is a starting point. Your response also depends on where the software runs, how it is exposed, and what an attacker could reach.
keywords: ← Back Home / Fieldnotes / Turn “critical” into a decision. THREAT PRIORITIZATION Turn “critical” into a decision. A published severity is a starting point. Your response also depends on where the software runs, how it is exposed, and what an attacker could reach. By Shai Zaidenberg · Practical perspective · 5 November 2026 Find the actual affected asset. Connect the advisory to a product, version, component, or image that exists in the environment. Distinguish a scanner match from evidence that the vulnerable functionality is present and reachable. Use context you can demonstrate. Exploitation evidence, internet exposure, asset importance, and verified controls help explain a priority. Do not assume a control is effective simply because a product is installed. Record unknowns and the evidence needed to resolve them. End with ownership and verification. The useful result is an action someone can carry out: an affected resource, an owner, an appropriate timeframe, and a check that proves the fix is active. A merged change and a remediated running service are different milestones. These are general engineering principles, not an assessment of a particular organization. Validate assumptions against your environment. Back to all insights

title: A quiet detection needs an explanation.
description: No alerts can mean no activity. It can also mean missing logs, a schema change, or a rule that no longer matches reality.
keywords: ← Back Home / Fieldnotes / A quiet detection needs an explanation. DETECTION ENGINEERING A quiet detection needs an explanation. No alerts can mean no activity. It can also mean missing logs, a schema change, or a rule that no longer matches reality. By Shai Zaidenberg · Practical perspective · 5 November 2026 Start with the data, not the counter. Before changing a silent detection, establish that its source is still producing events. Check the last event time, the collection path, and whether expected fields are populated. A zero on a dashboard is an observation; it is not yet an explanation. Test the logic against known behavior. Use a representative positive example and a benign negative example. Confirm that the rule matches the intended behavior without catching unrelated activity. When the schema changes, review the mapping rather than simply broadening the query. Keep the review loop small. Record what changed, why it changed, and what evidence demonstrated the result. Stage the improvement, monitor the outcome, and retain a way to restore the previous rule. Detection quality is ongoing engineering. These are general engineering principles, not an assessment of a particular organization. Validate assumptions against your environment. Back to all insights

title: Privacy
description: Privacy information for Shai Zaidenberg’s personal website.
keywords: ← Back Home / Privacy PRIVACY A small digital footprint. Updated 15 November 2026 What the site does This is Shai Zaidenberg’s personal cybersecurity website. It has no advertising, analytics, tracking pixels, embedded social widgets, or contact forms. Its own code does not set cookies. Images, video, fonts, styles, and scripts are served with the site. Your display preferences Theme, text size, contrast, spacing, underlining, and motion choices are stored locally in this browser. They are not sent to me. You can reset them in the accessibility panel or remove them in your browser’s site-data settings. The CISA news feed The news page requests a public JSON catalog from raw.githubusercontent.com, CISA’s official GitHub data mirror, when you open it or choose Refresh. GitHub receives the connection information required to serve that request, including your IP address. The request sends no login credentials and no referrer. Search and filter values stay in the page and are not transmitted. If the request fails, the page uses a dated bundled snapshot. There is no automatic background polling. Learning tools Playbook checkmarks and glossary searches remain in the current page. They are not saved to storage or sent to a server. Navigating away or reloading resets the playbook checkmarks. The Analyst Toolkit Everything you paste or type into the toolkit is processed by scripts running in this page. Indicators, tokens, encoded text, message headers, and network ranges are never transmitted, logged, or stored, and they disappear when you leave or reload the page. The hash calculator reads a file you choose inside your browser and does not upload it. The KEV check downloads the public catalog snapshot from this website and compares it locally, so the CVE IDs you enter are not sent anywhere. A Copy button writes to your clipboard only when you press it. Treat real tokens, credentials, and confidential incident data with care on any website, including this one. Homepage figures, diagrams, and films The exploitation figures on the homepage are read from a small summary file served by this website. For privacy questions or requests about messages you have sent, contact shaizaidenberg@gmail.com . title: Security by Design
description: Architecture, data boundaries, browser safeguards, and limitations of this public website.
keywords: ← Back Home / Security by Design ENGINEERING NOTES / THIS WEBSITE Small surface. Clear boundaries. Security is a set of design decisions and verification habits. Here are the choices behind this public website, and what they do—and do not—provide. 01 / ARCHITECTURE A static, public notebook. GitHub Pages serves HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts. There are no sign-in flows, custom backend services, payment forms, or private API keys in this site. Every shipped asset is public. This reduces application complexity. It does not remove risks from hosting, repository access, browser behavior, or future content changes. 02 / DATA BOUNDARY Public data stays public. The news desk reads a bundled CISA KEV snapshot and attempts a fresh copy from CISA’s official GitHub mirror. It validates the structure and shows the catalog date. A scheduled job in the public repository refreshes the bundled snapshot from the same official source, and only after the same validation and the site checks pass. If the request fails, the dated snapshot remains available. Searches, checklist inputs, and everything pasted into the Analyst Toolkit are processed in your browser. They are not submitted to a server. Theme and reading preferences use local browser storage. Read the privacy notice ↗ 03 / BROWSER SAFEGUARDS Keep the sources narrow. A Content Security Policy limits scripts, styles, fonts, images, and media to this site. Network requests are limited to this site and the official data mirror. Scripts are separate files; feed values and toolkit results are rendered as text, not executable HTML. Decoded content is displayed, never run. The policy is delivered in HTML. GitHub Pages controls HTTP headers, so this site does not claim complete control over server-level protections. 04 / AI & EVIDENCE Examples, without implied access. Agent walkthroughs are handcrafted fictional examples. They do not invoke AI models, query an organization, or perform response actions. Conceptual visuals do not depict an actual workplace. In operational systems, tool permissions, source provenance, human review, and outcome verification require their own implementation and testing. Read the editorial policy ↗ 05 / ACCESSIBILITY Motion is a choice. Pause animations, including the ambient background and diagram walkthroughs, using the control in the header or the accessibility panel. System reduced-motion preferences take priority. The site also offers light and dark themes, larger text, higher contrast, link underlining, and text spacing. Keyboard and responsive checks support the design. They are not a substitute for a comprehensive assistive-technology audit. View accessibility information ↗ 06 / REPORTING Found something to improve? For an accessibility problem, broken link, or suspected security issue, email Shai with the affected page and a concise description. Please avoid including credentials, personal records, or sensitive operational data. Email Shai ↗
